description: We combine software development with AI-driven visual storytelling. Our focus is building a working solution and presenting it clearly
summary:
Baseline is a visual health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long-duration missions, built by Team Codeshena for the moment when Earth is too far to answer in real time. NASA's challenge notes that on long missions astronauts must spot health changes in themselves. Baseline helps them do that: it compares each daily reading to the astronaut's own personal baseline instead of population averages, detects patterns across several indicators before any single value becomes critical, and tells the astronaut what to do next. Escalation adapts to the mission. On the ISS it says to contact the flight surgeon now; on a Mars transit, with up to 22 minutes one-way delay, it gives onboard steps and queues a report for Earth. This matters because the farther crews travel, the more they must act as their own first responders.
Live app: https://baseline-astronaut-health.vercel.app/
details:
What it does:

Baseline collects daily health indicators (heart rate, heart recovery/HRV, blood pressure, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, mood, fatigue, exercise) plus a 1-minute alertness (reaction-time) test inspired by NASA's PVT used on the ISS. It then shows the astronaut, in plain language, how they are doing and what to do.

How it works:

1.    Personal baseline: days 1–7 of the mission set each astronaut's "normal" for every indicator.

2.    Deviation: each new reading is compared to that personal normal and labelled Normal, Watch or Alert. Only the harmful direction counts (e.g. less sleep, slower reaction time).

3.    Persistence: a single odd reading asks for a re-measurement; 3 days in a row is flagged as a persistent change.

4.    Pattern detection: if at least 3 of 4 fatigue signals (sleep, HRV, reaction time, self-rated fatigue) drift the wrong way for 3 days, a "fatigue pattern" is raised even when no single value is critical.

5.    Spacewalk (EVA) readiness: Ready / Review first / Not recommended, always with the reasons. Final decision stays with the crew and flight surgeon.

6.    Mission-aware escalation: ISS (live link), Moon (seconds of delay) and Mars transit (minutes of delay, report queued with a live countdown).

Screens: Status (one-line summary, interactive body map of 5 body systems, spacewalk readiness, "what to do now"), Trends (14-day charts against the personal normal band), Check-in (daily form, alertness test and daily checklist), Report to Earth (auto-generated report for the flight surgeon). A Science & sources panel maps every indicator to a NASA Human Research Program risk.

Benefits and goals: Earlier detection of cumulative problems such as fatigue, clear explainable alerts, and safer decisions when ground support is delayed. All rules are transparent and deterministic. It is decision support only, never a diagnosis, and thresholds are configurable by the medical team. All demo data is simulated and clearly labelled.

Tools and technologies: Web app built with React, TypeScript and Vite, styled with Tailwind CSS, charts with Recharts, deployed on Vercel. Development was assisted by AI coding tools (Claude). No hardware was used; device input is simulated.
